Guides

Introducing allergens

Delaying peanut, egg, and milk does not prevent allergy. For most babies the safer plan is to start them, in a safe texture, and keep them coming.

Findings

Start the common allergens when solids start. That means around six months for most babies, and not before four months.
Regular peanut from infancy cut peanut allergy sharply in high-risk children. The LEAP trial found about an 80 percent relative reduction by age five in children with severe eczema or egg allergy.
Some babies should meet peanut only after a clinician agrees. Severe eczema, an existing egg allergy, or both is the group. Do not experiment past a worried doctor.
A contact rash around the mouth is not the same as anaphylaxis. Breathing trouble, floppiness, widespread hives, or repeated vomiting after a food is an emergency.

What changed in the evidence

For years families were told to delay peanut, egg, and fish. That advice matched rising allergy rates and did not cause them to fall. ESPGHAN now says allergenic foods may be introduced when complementary feeding begins, any time after four months. The practical age for a healthy baby is when solids start, around six months.

The foods that deserve a plan are peanut, egg, cow’s milk, wheat, sesame, fish, soy, and tree nuts. Shellfish can join that list once you are ready to offer it fully cooked and finely chopped. Introduce them in an edible form, not as a hidden trace, and keep serving them.

LEAP, EAT, and the guidelines that followed

LEAP enrolled infants at high risk because of severe eczema, egg allergy, or both. Those who ate peanut regularly until age five were far less likely to have peanut allergy than those who avoided it. The EAT trial offered six allergens from three months to breastfed infants from the general population. Protection was clearest in the children who actually ate the foods often enough, which many families found hard.

The US addendum guideline turned LEAP into practice: high-risk infants are considered for peanut between four and six months after other solids have shown the baby is ready, often with testing first. Infants with mild or moderate eczema are offered peanut around six months. Infants with no eczema can have it with the rest of the diet. European guidance is in the same direction.

How to do the first tastes

Pick a morning when the child is well, not the day of a vaccine or a fever. Offer a small amount of one new allergen, and stay nearby. Smooth peanut butter thinned into yogurt or fruit is the right peanut texture. A spoon of thick peanut butter can block the airway. Baked egg and hard-boiled egg both count; the yolk and white should be set. Tahini thinned into a dip is the right sesame texture.

If the first taste is tolerated, repeat it, and then keep it in the week. Stopping for months after one successful taste is how a planned introduction quietly becomes avoidance. A baby with severe eczema or a known egg allergy should be assessed before peanut. That assessment is a clinician’s job, and it may include a skin test or a supervised feed.

Rashes, illness, and emergencies

Drool plus a new acid fruit often reddens the chin. That contact irritation fades and is not an allergy work-up by itself. Hives that spread, swelling of the lips or tongue, vomiting, a hoarse cry, wheeze, or a baby who becomes pale and floppy needs emergency care. Antihistamine is not the treatment for breathing difficulty.

Do not use the weeks of an illness to diagnose an allergy from one meal, and do not start a brand-new allergen on a day the child is already unwell. After a true allergic reaction, the food stays out until a specialist has a plan. Home challenge tests are a bad idea.
